trajectory_rationale: Input-cost volatility and branded pricing actions are already explicitly linked at F1; later filings repeat pricing/pass-through as the same cost-recovery mechanism.

F1 contains category-level net pricing, but F5 materially sharpens the mechanism: reduced promotional activity plus a specific Jif peanut-butter list-price increase raises net sales by four percentage points.
Revenue-growth management and pricing/promotional discipline are present from F1 but remain broad and do not become a new concrete customer-economic mechanism by F5.

U.S./Canada price increases are already implemented and quantified at F1/F2; by F5 the filing mainly describes standing promotional/list-price mechanics rather than a new or strengthened yield action.
Protecting margins through price increases and favorable pricing variance are explicit at F1 and remain a persistent established yield mechanism through F5.
The company states from F1 that it introduces products at higher prices and increases prices to offset cost increases; materially the same cost-transfer language persists through F5.
Premiumization, higher-end Power Brand concentration and favorable pricing are explicit at F1 and repeated at F5; strong but static existing-customer yield strategy.
Pricing actions and favorable price/mix are operating drivers at F1 and remain higher-price/mix drivers at F5 without a new mechanism.

F1 explicitly states the objective to offset commodity increases with pricing and recover higher operating/labor costs through pricing; later filings show pass-through of raw-material/livestock costs. The mechanism is already fully explicit at F1.
Pricing actions and actual price increases already contribute to sales and earnings at F1; F5 continues to define price/mix as company pricing actions, so intensity is high but static.
Pricing and promotional effectiveness are present as established revenue-management levers, but the frozen F5 evidence does not rise to a sufficiently specific Strong customer-economic action.
Commodity and freight prices primarily reflect market/contract mechanics rather than a company-originated qualifying customer-yield or cost-transfer action.

Revenue-growth management and favorable price mix are explicit at F1; F5 expressly defines pricing actions by the company/bottlers as a price-mix driver. The mechanism is persistent rather than newly accelerating.
Cost inflation and premium-product demand are discussed, but the frozen evidence does not establish a concrete company customer-transfer or yield action at F5.

F1 explicitly links commodity fluctuations to pricing actions and shows actual higher pricing; F5 repeats pricing actions as a cost-management lever and reports higher-pricing margin benefit. Strong but pre-existing.
The frozen filings do not identify a qualifying customer pricing, entitlement, migration or cost-transfer mechanism; accounting references to discontinued operations are non-qualifying.
